title: 96.8% Chance Of A Panda-Style Update Within A Month According To Prediction Model Signals via @sejournal, @TaylorDanRW
content:
Back in March this year, I talked about the possibility of another Florida-style update rollout, and now, as we’re further on in the year, it feels as though another type of update from Google’s past might be ready to manifest. Remember Panda?
From a prediction model I built, it is suggesting that an update in the next month is a 96.8% possibility in the next 30 days.
Panda rolled out in February 2011 and was a site-level quality classifier. Google trained it on human judgments of pages and sites, asking simple questions such as: would you trust this, would you give it a credit card, is it written by someone who knows the subject, is it original, does it exist to help a reader or to guess what might rank.
Amit Singhal and Matt Cutts described it that way in the weeks after launch.
The public guidance that followed was a list of questions about trust, redundancy, and whether a page added anything the results did not already have. None of it specified a word count, a link ratio, or a template for “quality.”
It was easier to jump to these kinds of conclusions, as what the industry saw was the wreckage.
See also: 6 Months with Panda: A Story of Complacency, Hard Decisions, and Recovery
Content farms and thin affiliate sites had been a working model, and they lost visibility, often across the whole domain rather than on a single page. From that pattern, people reverse-engineered the algorithm based on the symptoms and not the cause.
Short pages had been common on the sites that dropped, so length became the diagnosis. Five hundred words hardened into a minimum, then a target, then a proxy for quality itself.
A page that answered a narrow question in 150 words was treated as defective. A page that repeated the same claim for two thousand words was treated as fixed. Length was observable, and not something Panda was scoring, and “thin pages” became a synonym for quality.
The deeper error was treating quality and length as intrinsic properties of a document, as Panda did not measure a page in isolation and award points for mass.
It separated sites that looked, to raters, like something a person would rely on from sites that looked like inventory. A long page can fail that test and a short one can pass it. The classifier was aimed at the character of the site, not at a threshold a writer could hit by padding.
See also: Google’s Answer on Ideal Content Length for SEO
When my prediction model evaluated the 25-year dataset of Google updates, alongside the confirmed rollout calendar for 2026, it showed a strong indication for a major official algorithm update before the end of the year (2026).
Google has not run a broad Core Update since May 2026 (updates in August and September were targeted spam updates ) and with Google typically running three to four major core updates per year, we are overdue.
This is the prime window. Once the September spam update completes its rollout, Google has an ideal 3- to 4-week window to push a broad core update and allow it to finish before Thanksgiving/Black Friday week.
According to my model, there is a 96.8% change of a Google Update in the next 30 days, and a longer forecast of 90.9% (confidence) over the next 90 days (from October 13th).
Historically, December updates are restricted to lighter link/spam updates ( such as December 2022/2023 ) or unconfirmed shifts. A major core update launching in December is rare due to the code freeze for the holiday retail season, though not completely unheard of.
To understand the likelihood of Google rolling out a confirmed update, I blend two key predictive signals:
A gradient-boosted decision tree model is then trained on past events to find the patterns between those signals, outputting calibrated probability scores for whether an unconfirmed tremor or an official rollout will trigger in the coming days.
Google’s guidance on AI content now says it is critical to manually fact-check and review everything generated before publishing, including titles, meta descriptions, structured data, and alt text, while the helpful-content guidelines have been given new language that defines main content and names the four things quality raters look for – effort, originality, talent or skill, and accuracy.
Mass-producing AI content without oversight is now cited as an example of little to no effort, which happens to be the single biggest culprit behind the sites I have seen hit by algorithm updates this year. Fake authors have been called a form of deception, with AI-generated headshots, made-up names, and false credentials named explicitly as a signal of a low-quality page.
Google has also been very public with its stance. At Search Central Live in Barcelona this week , and at Search Central Live in Bangkok last year , Gary Illyes said scaled content is becoming more of a problem than link spam.
A grizzlier Panda would not be a word-count rule under a new name, but the same kind of site-level classifier Google trained in 2011, aimed this time at pages produced to rank, authors who do not exist, and listicles placed to steer an answer rather than to help a reader.
Stakeholders should be told now that a broad core update is overdue; the documentation has already been rewritten around effort, originality, skill, and accuracy. A quality recalibration of scaled content (like Gary said in public) is more likely to land before the end of the year than after it, and the damage will sit on the site rather than on the thin page.
It’s time to prepare for a significant end to the year.

title: Coywolf Pack EmDash SEO Plugin Makes Sites Absurdly Fast via @sejournal, @martinibuster
content:
A new EmDash plugin was released that provides website management, performance, and SEO capabilities that are missing in EmDash. Despite all the features it adds, the plugin pack makes websites “absurdly fast.” The plugin is modular, enabling users to take advantage of only the functionalities they need.
There are many people who are using AI to generate all manner of plugins and software but the developer of the Coywolf pack, Jon Henshaw, is an acknowledged SEO expert with over 30 years of experience.
Henshaw is currently the Director of Audience Management at Yahoo, and has previously worked as the Head of SEO at CNET, Vimeo, plus managed global SEO for Paramount+, Pluto TV, and Showtime. Henshaw also developed the Raven Tools SEO platform that was acquired in 2017.
There is hardly anyone in the SEO industry who is as respected as Henshaw and has the level of trustworthiness and experience that he brings to his Coywolf Pack for EmDash. As you will see, the Coywolf Pack supercharges EmDash-based websites with more functionalities and exceedingly high performance.
The plugin adds three categories of improvements and expanded capabilities
There are many significant additions to this category of improvements. However, many devs and site owners will likely appreciate the website backup and recovery feature, secure storage for files submitted through website forms, file downloads with usage tracking, and expanded content blocks.
Coywolf Pack also extends EmDash’s existing video capabilities with Cloudflare Stream hosting and management, video engagement tracking, and captions. It also adds automatic VideoObject structured data for videos managed through its Cloudflare Stream integration and a video XML sitemap.
There are also content blocks that call attention to important information, along with blocks for disclosures, quotes, testimonials, and podcast links.
What bears noting is that these features do not add bloat. I tested the home page and inner web pages, including the category page for videos and a page with a video on it, and they all achieved perfect PageSpeed Insights scores of 100.
Coywolf Pack improves EmDash’s SEO capabilities with expanded crawler controls and structured data, stronger focus on aiding search engine content discovery, metadata generation, link and redirect management, and other features that add to or vastly improve EmDash’s built-in SEO features.
The Coywolf Pack WordPress migration module is an example of how it improves over the native function in EmDash. EmDash already has a WordPress Migration feature but it falls short of providing a perfect migration for real-world data imports.
Coywolf Pack’s WordPress Import module extends EmDash’s built-in importer to preserve content, URLs, redirects, and site relationships that might otherwise be lost during a WordPress to EmDash migration.
Here is how Coywolf Pack extends EmDash’s native WordPress importer:
Heading IDs Preserves existing heading anchor links so that links to specific sections of articles continue working (and showing up in Google search results).
Preserves Existing Redirects Converts old WordPress slugs and redirect rules from Yoast, Rank Math, and Redirection into EmDash redirects. EmDash’s native importer imports Yoast and Rank Math SEO titles and descriptions but there is no documentation about importing redirects from those three popular SEO and redirect plugins.
Comprehensive Media URL Importer Redirects legacy WordPress media URLs to the imported media library, including resized image variants and files outside WordPress’s media library. This goes beyond EmDash’s native media library importer, which is perfectly fine, but is missing this extra step which many publishers may need.
WordPress Import (Maintains Parent-Child Hierarchy) A successful site migration can often hinge on replicating an accurate one-to-one URL and site hierarchy relationships. Failure to perfectly replicate the old site can lead to delays and loss of ranking.
EmDash’s native WordPress importer creates imported categories at the top level but can lose their original parent-child relationships. So if you have this kind of hierarchical structure: News > Local> Article, the Coywolf Pack importer will preserve that parent-child relationship. The same issue affects WordPress pages that have parent pages. Coywolf Pack restores parent-child relationships between categories and pages.
The parent-child hierarchy feature works like this:
Co-Authors And Guest Authors This is an example of how Coywolf can handle niche but real-world WordPress import issues. EmDash imports authors and guest authors. Coywolf can handle multiple authors for an article, guest author profiles that don’t require user accounts.
Importantly, Coywolf Pack supports importing data from these popular WordPress plugins:
WordPress Blocks Migration Coywolf also supports migrating specific kinds of blocks that preserve their functionalities. It preserves reusable blocks, quotations, and expandable Details blocks. It also converts existing blocks from Coywolf’s WordPress plugins into corresponding Coywolf Pack blocks.
Coywolf Pack adds performance enhancements that extend EmDash’s existing capabilities, improving page speed, caching reliability, database efficiency, image delivery, and search responsiveness. It also automates performance management and reduces server and browser processing, helping publishers deliver faster websites with less maintenance.
EmDash is already well known for delivering fast websites. Henshaw describes the improvements from his Coywolf pack as bumping up his website to “absurdly fast” performance. He’s not exaggerating. I tested his site and it scores a perfect 100 in PageSpeed Insights.
Among the improvements is cache warming, which is the process of proactively caching web pages or resources before a website visitor requests them, which dramatically improves page speeds for those visitors. Normally a caching system doesn’t create a cache until a visitor first requests a web page but cache warming doesn’t wait around for a first visit. Cache warming proactively caches pages so their rendered HTML is ready cached before visitors arrive.
1. First Visits (Faster Page Delivery) Keeps pages cached for days while automatically clearing outdated content after deployments and relevant settings changes. Cached responses take 60–90 milliseconds instead of 1–2 seconds, according to Coywolf.
2. Clearing the Cache (Automated Cache Management) Clears affected cached content without unnecessarily clearing the entire website’s cache, preserving performance when settings or redirects change.
3. Cold Pages After a Clear (Automatic Cache Warming) Prepares cached pages after deployments, cache clearing, and content edits so visitors and crawlers are less likely to encounter slower, uncached pages.
4. Images (Image Delivery and Optimization) Delivers images directly from Cloudflare’s media infrastructure, with responsive sizing, long-term caching, and image dimensions specified in the HTML to prevent layout shifts and improve the Core Web Vitals Cumulative Layout Shift (CLS) scores.
5. Live Search (Faster Internal Search) This is an ingenious feature that improves the user experience. It provides instant search suggestions using a browser-based title index, cached search results, and fewer database queries.
6. Redirects (Faster URL Redirection) Processes redirects before EmDash renders pages. It caches the responses to reduce server processing.
7. Fewer D1 Round Trips (Database Optimization) Combines database queries, caches settings, and reuses retrieved information to reduce delays when generating uncached pages. It reduces the number of separate interactions with the database, helping uncached pages load faster.
Each database interaction (D1 round trip) costs approximately 25–30 milliseconds and these optimizations reduce the Coywolf pack’s database overhead when generating uncached pages.
8. No Client JavaScript Where It Isn’t Needed (Server-Side Rendering) Renders tables of contents, breadcrumbs, reviews, and structured data on the server, reducing the amount of rendering that has to be done on the browser side and increasing the speed at which pages load.
